newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK economy boasts robust first quarter growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK economy boasts robust first quarter growth.

text.p: Britain's economy grew by an annual three percent in the first quarter of the year, official data out on Friday showed, healthy growth by any standards but probably too late to save the beleaguered Conservative Party.

The Office for National Statistics said British gross domestic product rose 1.0 percent in the three months to March from the previous three and by 3.0 percent compared with the first quarter of 1996.
The last set of data before next Thursday's election showed economic growth is accelerating. The economy only grew 2.6 percent year-on-year in the fourth quarter.

Prime Minister John Major told a news conference Britain was set for sustained growth "as far ahead as you can credibly judge." He said the old-style boom/bust cycle had been banished forever, leaving Britain as the "economic envy of Europe."
Conservative strategists believe they are making headway against the opposition Labour Party on the economy and Europe.

But with the election only six days away and latest opinion polls putting Tony Blair's Labour about 16 to 18 points ahead, it could be a case of too little too late for the party that has been in power for 18 years.
If the polls prove correct, Labour's Gordon Brown will inherit the keys to the Treasury and a buoyant economy. The problem is it will need restraining sooner rather than later.

"The figures demonstrate that the economy remained buoyant during the first quarter," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc. "They do provide another argument for a degree of overall policy restraint."
Economists say "trend" economic growth runs between two and 2.5 percent on an annual basis. Any faster than that and the economy risks overheating, causing inflationary pressures.
"Today's GDP data suggest the economy is expanding at an above-trend pace and too quickly for compatibility with a 2.5 percent inflation objective," said Andy Cates, economist at UBS.
The Conservative government has a target of 2.5 percent for annual underlying inflation -- it was 2.7 percent in March -- and Brown has adopted the same goal.
He plans to overhaul the monetary structure, disbanding monthly meetings between Chancellor of the Exchequer and Bank of England Governor in favour of a broader committee of experts.

But before that happens, a meeting with Bank Governor Eddie George is tentatively pencilled in for May 7, just six days after polling day. Some economists expect Brown to raise rates there and then to establish his anti-inflationary credentials.
But others say the correct prescription for Britain's bubbling economy is not quite so simple, with the recovery split between booming services and retail and subdued manufacturing.

Friday's data showed the service sector storming ahead, up 3.9 percent year-on-year while the hard-pressed manufacturing industries grew only slightly faster than the fourth quarter, the ONS said. In the last three months of 1996, manufacturing output rose a meagre 0.7 percent on an annual basis.

The dilemma facing the next Chancellor is that manufacturers are struggling as the strength of the pound -- up about 17 percent since last August -- pushes up their export prices. And the higher rates go, the higher the pound is likely to soar.

"While the pace of overall growth is certain to increase calls for policy action to prevent overheating, sharp rises in interest rates would threaten to further unbalance growth by tipping industry back towards recession," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "A fiscal tightening would appear to be the correct policy prescription."
Brown has ruled out any increases in income tax rates or extensions of value added tax to many areas.

That still leaves a host of options such as corporation tax or tax relief on home loan payments. But many analysts expect the next Chancellor to plump for interest rate rises, rather than challenge the new British political dogma that headline taxes can only go one way -- down.
